title: Model Monitoring & Drift
summary: Catching a model quietly degrading in production, often before you even have new labels to measure accuracy directly.

slides.subTitle: The world changes, the code doesn't
slides.markdown: A deployed model is a **frozen snapshot** of patterns learned from historical data — but the real world keeps changing after training ends: customer behavior shifts, a competitor changes pricing, a new product category launches, a pandemic changes shopping habits overnight. None of that updates the model's weights. Unlike a typical software bug, this failure mode produces **no error, no crash, no exception** — the model keeps returning confident-looking predictions, just increasingly wrong ones, which is exactly why it's dangerous: nothing in standard application monitoring (uptime, error rates, latency) will catch it. This is the core reason ML systems need a category of monitoring that traditional software monitoring doesn't cover.

slides.subTitle: Input shift vs relationship shift
slides.markdown: **Data drift**: the distribution of **input features** changes, but the true relationship between features and the target stays the same — e.g. a fraud model starts seeing more transactions from a new country because the product just launched there, but "what makes a transaction fraudulent" hasn't actually changed. **Concept drift**: the relationship between features and the target itself changes — e.g. fraudsters adopt a new tactic, so the same feature pattern that used to indicate legitimate behavior now indicates fraud. The distinction matters for the fix: data drift can sometimes be handled by better feature coverage or re-weighting; concept drift generally requires retraining on new labeled data reflecting the new relationship, since the old labels no longer describe the current reality.

slides.subTitle: The earliest warning signal
slides.markdown: Tracking each input feature's distribution over time (mean, variance, or a formal distance metric like population stability index / KL divergence, comparing production data to the training distribution) is the earliest and cheapest drift signal available, because it requires **no labels at all** — you can compute it the instant a prediction request comes in. A sudden shift (a feature's average value jumps, a previously rare category becomes common) is a leading indicator that something about the world has changed, well before you'd have enough new labeled data to detect an accuracy drop directly. This is why feature-distribution monitoring is usually the first alerting layer set up, even before prediction or outcome monitoring.

slides.subTitle: Two more layers, still label-free
slides.markdown: Beyond input features, two more monitoring layers require no ground-truth labels either. **Prediction distribution monitoring**: track the model's output distribution over time — if a fraud model that historically flagged 2% of transactions suddenly flags 15%, something changed (in the data, the model, or the world), regardless of whether you know the true fraud rate yet. **Downstream business metric monitoring**: track metrics the model is meant to influence (chargebacks, revenue, click-through) — these lag further than prediction monitoring but are the ultimate signal, since a model can look statistically stable while still failing the actual business goal it exists to serve.

slides.subTitle: Scheduled vs drift-triggered
slides.markdown: **Scheduled retraining** (weekly, monthly) is simple and predictable but can be wasteful (retraining when nothing changed) or too slow (a fast-moving concept drift causing real harm for weeks before the next scheduled run). **Drift-triggered retraining** fires when monitoring detects meaningful drift, reacting faster to real change but requiring reliable drift detection to avoid false-alarm retrains, and reliable, timely access to fresh labeled data to retrain on. Many production systems combine both: a scheduled baseline cadence as a floor, with drift-triggered retraining as an early-warning override for fast-moving cases the schedule alone wouldn't catch in time.

slides.subTitle: Labels needed for accuracy arrive late or never
slides.markdown: It's tempting to think "just monitor live accuracy" — but for most production systems, the true label often arrives **days, weeks, or never** after the prediction. A loan-default model's "ground truth" (did they actually default?) may not be known for a year; a fraud model's confirmed label depends on a customer dispute process that can take weeks; a churn model's label is by definition only knowable after the fact. A monitoring strategy that depends solely on accuracy is a monitoring strategy that's **always looking backward at stale information**, or in the worst case, never gets a signal at all. This is exactly why feature-distribution and prediction-distribution monitoring (label-free, available instantly) matter — they're not a nice-to-have, they're often the *only* real-time signal available.
